newsitem.title: USA: Chemist alleges documents destroyed by tobacco maker.
newsitem.headline: Chemist alleges documents destroyed by tobacco maker.

text.p: Texas Attorney General Dan Morales on Thursday alleged Philip Morris Tobacco Co. destroyed incriminating documents on the health effects of smoking and used altered cigarettes in research tests.

In a deposition, 20-year Philip Morris analytical chemist Ray Morgan said he was ordered in the 1980s to shred research reports that showed "alarmingly high" concentrations of nitrosamine, a known carcinogen, in tobacco smoke, Morales said.

Morgan also testified the company, a unit of Philip Morris Cos. Inc., used "non-production" cigarettes with fewer chemical additives than cigarettes sold to consumers in research tests used to detect carcinogens, Morales said.

"This is devastating evidence against the tobacco industry, especially in regard to their racketeering activities," Morales said. "The more the industry fights, the more it becomes entangled in its own web of deception.

Morgan in the deposition taken in Richmond, Va., said he was asked by his boss at a Philip Morris lab there to shred results of his research into carcinogens in sidestream condensate -- the smoke coming off the lit end of cigarettes.
"I believe the evidence will show that he was mistaken," said Michael York, an attorney with Washington, D.C. law firm Wehner and York representing Philip Morris.
"The data he's testifying about was retained. Not only was it retained, but it was produced to Mr. Morales' coordinate plaintiffs in Minnesota, and Morales' private lawyer knows that," York said.
Texas is one of more than 20 states that have sued the tobacco industry seeking to recover costs of taxpayer-funded medical treatment of smokers.
Several states also have lodged antitrust and racketeering claims against the tobacco makers for allegedly concealing evidence of the health effects of smoking.

The first case, brought by Mississippi's attorney general, is set to go to trial in June in Pascagoula, Miss. The Texas lawsuit sought $4 billion in alleged Medicaid costs from the tobacco industry and is set for trial in September.
A spokesman for Morales said state officials have met with counterparts in a series of meetings across the country to discuss settling the massive litigation against the tobacco industry.

"I would say we would be closer to a settlement now than we were maybe a year ago, but we still have a long way to go before we could say that a settlement is around the corner," spokesman Ron Dusek said.

The tobacco companies earlier this week said they were not engaged in settlement talks, but a Wall Street analyst said the companies were likely to agree to be regulated by the government and pay into a settlement fund in exchange for a settlement protecting them from any future claims for illnesses caused by smoking.
